name: Absalom
title: David's rebellious son
summary: Absalom, David's third son by Maacah from the Aramean kingdom of Geshur, was renowned for his exceptional beauty and thick hair. When his half-brother Amnon raped their sister Tamar, Absalom harbored his hatred in silence for two years before orchestrating Amnon's murder at a sheep-shearing festival in Baal-Hazor. The following three years he spent in exile with his maternal grandfather King Talmai in Geshur. After a long process to regain his father's favor – first through Joab's scheme involving the wise woman from Tekoa, then after waiting two more years – Absalom devised a calculated plan to seize power. By stationing himself at Jerusalem's city gate and undermining trust in David's legal system, he systematically won the people's loyalty. The rebellion culminated when he had himself proclaimed king in Hebron, forcing David to flee his own capital. Theologically, the uprising can be understood as a fulfillment of Nathan's prophecy that the sword would never depart from David's house, as a consequence of the sin against Uriah and Bathsheba. Absalom's end came in the forest of Ephraim, where his head became caught in an oak tree and he was pierced by Joab – despite David's explicit order to spare him. David's heart-wrenching lament, "O my son Absalom, my son!" is one of Scripture's most moving expressions of a father's grief.

keyEvents.title: Revenge for Sister Tamar
keyEvents.description: After Amnon had raped Absalom's sister Tamar, Absalom waited two years before arranging the murder of Amnon during a sheep shearing in Baal-Hazor.

keyEvents.title: Flight to Geshur
keyEvents.description: After killing Amnon, Absalom fled to his maternal grandfather King Talmai in Geshur, where he lived in exile for three years.

keyEvents.title: Return to Jerusalem
keyEvents.description: Through Joab's trick with the wise woman from Tekoa, Absalom was granted permission to return to Jerusalem, but had to wait another two years before he could appear before his father again.

keyEvents.title: Building Popular Support
keyEvents.description: Absalom stationed himself at the city gate and undermined trust in David's legal system by promising justice to anyone who brought a case. In this way, he won the hearts of the people and laid the groundwork for his rebellion.

keyEvents.title: The Rebellion and the Capture of Jerusalem
keyEvents.description: Absalom had himself proclaimed king in Hebron and forced David to flee from Jerusalem. Following Ahithophel's advice, he took his father's concubines on the roof of the palace as a public sign of his seizure of power.

keyEvents.title: Absalom's Death in the Forest of Ephraim
keyEvents.description: During the battle in the Forest of Ephraim, Absalom's head became caught in a large oak tree. Joab pierced him with three spears, contrary to David's explicit order to spare him. David's lament over his son is among the most moving passages in all Scripture.

versions.summary: Absalom was King David's third son, born of Maacah, daughter of King Talmai of Geshur. He is best known for his rebellion against his own father to seize the throne of Israel, as well as for his exceptional beauty and especially his long, heavy hair. His tragic death brought great sorrow to David.

The correct role should be 'prince'.; [minor] The role 'rebel' should be added to reflect his most well-known action – the rebellion against King David.; [minor] The event concerning the conquest of Jerusalem and the concubines should also include reference to 2 Sam 16:20-22 (bookId 10, chapter 16) where Absalom takes David's concubines following Ahithophel's advice.; [minor] Traditionally, the text in 2 Sam 18:9 states that Absalom's head became caught in the oak tree (not explicitly his hair). That it was his hair is a very widespread tradition, but the Bible text mentions 'the head'. It may be appropriate to nuance the description.; [minor] According to 2 Sam 14:27, Absalom had three sons in addition to his daughter Tamar. The sons are not named, but it can be mentioned that he had several children.; [major] Footnotes are missing. The profile should include footnotes covering historical, linguistic, and theological aspects of Absalom.; [minor] Absalom was married – he had children, which presupposes a spouse. Although the name is not given in the Bible, this can be noted.

versions.summary: Absalom was King David's third son, born to Maacah, daughter of King Talmai of Geshur. He is best known for his rebellion against his own father to seize the throne in Israel, as well as for his exceptional beauty and especially his long, heavy hair. Absalom's rebellion can be understood theologically as a fulfillment of the prophet Nathan's judgment on David's house after the sin with Bathsheba. His tragic death in the forest of Ephraim brought deep grief to David, who lamented: "My son Absalom, my son, my son Absalom! If only I had died instead of you!"

versions.reason: [minor] The summary is very similar to version 1 (starting identically: 'Absalom was King David's third son, born of Maacah, daughter of King Talmai of Geshur. He is best known...'). Since an earlier version exists, the text should be rephrased more clearly to distinguish it from the previous attempt.; [minor] The Bible text states that Absalom's hair got caught in the oak tree, not his head. 2 Sam 18:9 says 'his head' was caught, but this is traditionally interpreted as meaning his hair became entangled. The phrasing 'Absalom's head hanging fast' is imprecise—it should clarify that it was his hair that got stuck, or possibly that he was left suspended between heaven and earth.; [minor] According to 2 Sam 14:27, Absalom had three sons in addition to his daughter Tamar. Although the names of the sons are not mentioned, it may be worth noting this, or at least avoiding any implication that Tamar was his only child.; [minor] Absalom evidently had a wife (or wives), since he had children (2 Sam 14:27), yet spouse is set to zero. Although the wife is not named in the Bible, this should be noted.; [minor] 'Warrior' is acceptable, but Absalom might more precisely be described as a 'military commander' or 'strategist' in connection with his rebellion. The role of 'judge' (self-appointed) could also be considered, given his conduct at the city gate where he promised justice.; [minor] The footnote's source is labeled 'archaeological', but its content primarily concerns a textual tension in the biblical text. The well-known 'Absalom's Pillar' in the Kidron Valley dates to the 1st century BC (Hellenistic/Hasmonean period) and is not the original pillar erected by Absalom. It should be clarified that the current monument in the Kidron Valley does not date from Absalom's time.; [minor] According to rabbinic tradition in Sotah 10b, Absalom was pierced by three spears/staves of Joab (cf. 2 Sam 18:14), not ten. The number ten relates to the story about his concubine, but the direct connection 'pierced by ten spears' is imprecise in representing the rabbinic source. Check the exact wording in Sotah 10b.

versions.summary: Absalom, David's third son by Maacah from the Aramean kingdom of Geshur, was known for his striking beauty and impressive hair. When his half-brother Amnon raped their sister Tamar, Absalom waited patiently for two years before taking blood vengeance and killing Amnon. After three years in exile in Geshur and a long process to regain his father's favor, Absalom launched a systematic rebellion, winning the people's hearts at Jerusalem's city gate and finally having himself proclaimed king in Hebron. David was forced to flee from his own capital. The rebellion, which can be seen theologically as a fulfillment of Nathan's prophecy concerning the consequences of David's sin with Bathsheba, ended with Absalom's death in the forest of Ephraim – where he became caught by his hair in an oak tree and was killed by Joab against David's explicit wish. David's heart-wrenching lament over his son ranks among the most moving scenes in the Hebrew Bible.

Consider using 'Scripture' for consistency with the language used in keyEvents.; [major] According to 2 Sam 14:27, Absalom had three sons (whose names are not mentioned) and one daughter named Tamar. The profile mentions only the daughter. Although the sons are unnamed, this should be noted or the children field should reflect that there were multiple children. Alternatively, one could keep only Tamar as the sole named child, but this should at least be commented on.; [minor] The list of siblings is representative but not complete – David had many more children than those listed. The list includes the most relevant ones (especially Amnon, Tamar, Adonijah and Solomon), but it could have been useful to be consistent. Kileab is sometimes written as 'kileab' – ensure that the id matches what is used elsewhere in the system.; [minor] The text says that Absalom got caught 'by his hair' in an oak tree, but the Hebrew base text of 2 Sam 18:9 states that his head (rosho) was caught in the oak. It is the rabbinic tradition (mentioned in the footnote) that connects this to his hair. It may be more precise to say 'his head got caught' in the event itself, and leave the interpretation about his hair for the footnote.; [minor] 'Commander' is somewhat misleading for Absalom. He led a rebellion and had an army, but he appointed Amasa as his commander (2 Sam 17:25). 'Claimant to the throne' or 'rival king' would have been more precise.; [minor] The summary is very good, but since this is the third version and scores should be higher, one must ensure that the wording is clearly distinct from earlier versions, both of which began with 'Absalom was King David's third son, born to Maacah, daughter of King Talmai of Geshur'.

footnotes.text: The name Absalom (Hebrew: אַבְשָׁלוֹם, Avshalom) means 'my father is peace' or 'father of peace' – an ironic name given his violent life and rebellion against his own father David.

In 2 Sam 18:18 it is mentioned that Absalom erected a memorial pillar in the King's Valley because he said he had no son to keep his name in memory. However, the well-known monument in the Kidron Valley near Jerusalem traditionally called 'Absalom's Pillar' dates from the first century BC and is therefore not the original monument. The biblical account stands in tension with 2 Sam 14:27, which mentions three sons – suggesting that they may have died young.

Absalom's rebellion has deep theological parallels to Nathan's prophecy in 2 Sam 12:10–12, where it is foretold that the sword shall never depart from David's house and that one from his own household will take his wives in full public view – as a direct consequence of David's sin with Bathsheba and the murder of Uriah.

Geshur, to which Absalom fled after killing Amnon, was a small Aramean kingdom in the northeastern Golan region. David's marriage to Maacah, daughter of King Talmai of Geshur, was likely a political alliance that secured David's northeastern border.

In rabbinic tradition (Babylonian Talmud, Sotah 10b), Absalom's fate is used as a classic example of middah keneged middah – that one reaps what one sows. He was proud of his beautiful hair, and it was precisely his hair that caused his downfall. The tradition explains how his vanity and rebellion against his father led to his ruin.

Absalom's strategy of standing at the city gate and promising justice (2 Sam 15:2–6) reflects a known political tactic in the ancient Near East. The city gate was the central place for legal proceedings and public administration, and by undermining trust in the king's judicial system, Absalom positioned himself as an alternative to his father.

The Hebrew text of 2 Sam 18:9 uses the word 'rosho' (his head), not 'se'aro' (his hair), regarding what became caught in the oak. The idea that it was his hair that got stuck originates from rabbinic tradition and has become part of popular storytelling, but strictly speaking, it is an interpretive tradition rather than a direct rendering of the original text.
